displayQuote: It is better to be feared than loved, if you cannot be both

meta.title: Who really said "It is better to be feared than loved, if you cannot be both"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it is Machiavelli, from The Prince (Ch. 17, 1532). But the pithy wording is a paraphrase, and it strips out his point that a prince should aim to be both.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It is better to be feared than loved, if you cannot be both'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Machiavelli, from The Prince Chapter 17 (1532) — but the popular wording condenses his longer, more qualified sentence.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1469–1527 · Florentine statesman & political theorist; The Prince written c.1513, published 1532
answer.sourceLine: Genuinely Machiavelli: the line condenses a passage in The Prince, Chapter 17, which asks “whether it be better to be beloved than feared” and concludes it is “much more safe to be feared than to be loved, when you have to choose between the two.” The pithy “if you cannot be both” wording is a modern paraphrase of his longer, more qualified sentence.

source.heading: The primary source

docMeta.dd: Chapter 17 — “Of Cruelty and Clemency, and Whether It Is Better to Be Loved Than Feared”

source.excerpt: From this arises the question whether it be better to be beloved than feared, or to be feared than beloved. … It is much more safe to be feared than to be loved, when you have to choose between the two.
trail: The full chapter is online at Wikisource (Detmold translation) ↗, which confirms “much more safe to be feared than to be loved.”
Yale SOM’s “No, Machiavelli Did Not Say It’s Better to Be Feared Than Loved” ↗ notes the popular version strips his advice to be both loved and feared.
The complete Marriott translation is at Project Gutenberg ↗.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version compresses this into “if you cannot be both”
source.excerptNote: Machiavelli’s fuller point is that a prince should wish to be both loved and feared, and choose fear only when the two cannot be combined — a nuance the shortened quote tends to drop.
source.rightsNote: Machiavelli’s text (1532) and all standard English translations quoted here are long in the public domain.

author.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
author.heading: About Niccolò Machiavelli
author.bio: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat, historian and political philosopher who served the Republic of Florence until the Medici returned to power in 1512. Out of office, he wrote The Prince (c.1513), a hard-eyed manual on acquiring and holding power that gave us the adjective “Machiavellian.” The book was printed in 1532, five years after his death.

misattribution.heading: The real misunderstanding
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Machiavelli is correct — the trouble is with the wording and the meaning. The popular one-liner is a paraphrase that flattens a more careful argument.

items.why: “If you cannot be both” is a modern condensation. Machiavelli’s sentence in The Prince Ch. 17 runs “it is much more safe to be feared than to be loved, when you have to choose between the two” (Wikisource ↗). He wrote in Italian; every English form is a translator’s wording.

items.who: a blanket endorsement of ruling by fear
items.why: Machiavelli says a prince should aim to be both loved and feared, choosing fear only if forced — and warns above all to avoid being hated. Yale SOM argues the quotable version corrupts this into the false lesson that cruelty is always necessary (Yale Insights ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Bottom line: it really is Machiavelli, from The Prince Ch. 17 — but read the whole sentence, which says a prince should want to be both loved and feared and pick fear only when he must (Wikisource ↗).

context.heading: Why the line endures
lead: Chapter 17 is the emotional core of The Prince: Machiavelli coolly weighs love against fear as instruments of rule and decides fear is the safer bet, because love “is preserved by the link of obligation which… is broken at every opportunity,” while fear is held by “a dread of punishment which never fails.”
But he immediately hedges: the wise prince makes himself feared without becoming hated. The famous soundbite keeps the cold calculation and loses the caution.
context.pull: One should wish to be both — but if forced to choose, it is safer to be feared.
